en: Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya, Volume One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
I bow my head to the author of this treatise, who was born from the very body of the Sugata, as well as to our teacher who taught us; I shall now diligently elucidate its meaning.
Herein, first, the essential nature of the treatise is established.
The verse says:
Only the obscuration of the true nature, And the cultivation of its various remedies—
These very stages of cultivation Result in the attainment of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.

The Commentary states: This treatise explains only these seven topics: first, the characteristics; second, the hindrances; third, reality; fourth, the cultivation of various remedies; fifth, the stages of this very cultivation; sixth, the attainment of the fruit; and seventh, the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
Now, within this context, its characteristics are first explained.
The verse says:
"False imagination exists; Within it, both [subject and object] are entirely absent."
"Herein there is only emptiness; therein also this exists.
The Commentary says:
"The existence of false discrimination" refers to the discrimination of the grasped object and the grasping subject.
"That both of these are entirely non-existent" means that within this very false discrimination, there is forever an absence of the two natures of the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka).
"In this, there is only emptiness" means that within false discrimination, there exists only the emptiness that is the absence of the grasped and the grasper.
"That there is also this in that" means that within those two types of emptiness, there is likewise only this false conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
If something is not present therein, it is seen as empty by virtue of that absence;
yet because what remains is not non-existent, it is known as existing in accordance with reality.
If it is thus, one will be able to correctly demonstrate the characteristic of emptiness.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Therefore, all phenomena are said to be neither empty nor non-empty."
Because of existence, non-existence, and the fact that [existence] exists, this accords with the Middle Way.
The treatise says:
"All phenomena" refers to all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
False conceptualization is called the conditioned, while the emptiness of the two graspings is called the unconditioned.

Based on the reasoning stated above, it is said that all these phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty: they are said to be "not empty" because false conceptualization exists as emptiness, and they are said to be "not non-empty" because the nature of the grasped and the grasper does not exist.
"Because it exists" means that emptiness exists within false discrimination.
"Because it does not exist" means that the two natures of the grasped and the grasper do not exist.
Furthermore, "because it exists" means that emptiness exists within false discrimination, and false discrimination exists within emptiness.

This is what it means to accord with the Middle Way: that all phenomena are neither exclusively empty nor exclusively non-empty. Such a principle perfectly accords with the Middle Way and is well in harmony with the teachings of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, which state that all phenomena are neither empty nor existent.
Thus, having already demonstrated that false discrimination possesses both aspects—the aspect of existence and the aspect of non-existence—their specific characteristics shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Consciousness arises and transforms, appearing as objects, Sentient beings, a self, and cognition.
This object does not truly exist; because the object is absent, consciousness is absent.
The commentary says:
"Transforming into what resembles an object" means that it manifests as having the nature of various objects such as form and so forth.
"Transforming into that which resembles sentient beings" means appearing as the nature of the five sense faculties of oneself and others.
"Transforming into that which resembles a self" means that the afflicted *manas* is constantly associated with self-delusion (*ātma-moha*) and the other [afflictions].
"That which appears as the cognizer" refers to the other six consciousnesses, because their mode of cognition is coarse.

"This object is not actually existent" means that what appears as the object and what appears as the sense faculty lack cognitive aspects (*ākāra*); likewise, what appears as the self and what appears as the cognizer are not true manifestations, and thus none of them are substantially real.

"Because the object is absent, consciousness is absent" means that because the four objects, such as the apprehended meaning (*grāhyārtha*), are absent, the various consciousnesses that apprehend them (*grāhakavijñāna*) are also not substantially real.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The nature of false discrimination (*abhūtaparikalpa-svabhāva*) is established by virtue of this principle.
"It is neither substantially existent nor entirely non-existent, for its cessation and liberation are admitted.
The Commentary says:
"False imagination is established as non-substantially existent by virtue of this meaning, because that which arises as it appears is not truly real."
Nor is it entirely non-existent, because within it there arises a slight degree of deluded consciousness.
Why do you not allow that this nature is entirely non-existent?
For you admit that by its cessation one attains liberation.
If it were otherwise, both bondage and liberation would be non-existent; thus, one would fall into the error of negating both defilement and purification.
Having already revealed the self-characteristic of false discrimination, its inclusive characteristic shall now be explained.
The mere existence of such false conceptualization is itself capable of fully encompassing the three natures.
The verse says:
"Only the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected nature."
"Because of the object, because of conceptualization, and because of the emptiness of both, it is so taught.
The treatise says:
Based upon the objects of false conceptualization, the existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is taught.
Based on the nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is said to exist;
based on the emptiness of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka-śūnyatā*), the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is said to exist.

Having already clarified the characteristics subsumed under false conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*), one should now explain the characteristic of the skillful means for entering the signless (*animitta*) within that very false conceptualization.
The verse says:
Based on the apprehension of consciousness, The non-apprehension of objects arises.
"Based on the non-apprehension of objects, the non-apprehension of consciousness arises.
The commentary states:
Because one relies upon the apprehension of what exists as mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), there first arises the non-apprehension of external objects.
Furthermore, because there is non-apprehension of the object, there subsequently arises non-apprehension of consciousness.
By means of this expedient, one enters into the signlessness of the grasped and the grasper.
Furthermore, the verse says:
Because consciousness possesses the nature of attainment, It also becomes non-attainment;
Thus one knows that the two—attainment and non-attainment— Are equal in their nature of non-attainment.
The treatise states:
Because consciousness, when arising, manifests as various kinds of false objects, it is said to "possess apprehension.
Since the apprehended objects lack real intrinsic nature, the real intrinsic nature of the apprehending subject cannot be established either.

Because the consciousness that is capable of apprehending finds nothing to be apprehended, both the apprehended object and the apprehending subject—which were previously considered objects of attainment—equally become of the nature of non-apprehension.
Having thus revealed the characteristic of the skillful means for entering the signlessness of false discrimination, the characteristics of its various distinct categories shall now be explained.
The verse says:
The mind and mental factors of the three realms Are false conceptualization.
That which merely cognizes an object is called "mind," And those that are distinct from it are called "mental factors."
The treatise states:

Regarding the characteristics of the distinctions of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), these consist of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

Regarding their alternative designations (*paryāya-lakṣaṇa*): that which can cognize only the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of objects is termed "mind" (*citta*); furthermore, that which also cognizes specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is termed the various mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth.
Now, the characteristics of its arising shall be explained.
The verse says:
One is called the consciousness that conditions; the second is named the experiencer.
Among these, that which experiences is the mind, while discrimination and investigation are mental factors (*caitta*).
The commentary states:
"That which takes objects as its condition" refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), because it serves as the generative condition for the other consciousnesses.

The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which arise with the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) as their condition, are called "experiencers" because they are the subjects that experience.

Among these various consciousnesses, sensation (*vedanā*) is able to experience, perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to differentiate, and mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) such as volition (*cetanā*) and attention (*manasikāra*) are able to impel the consciousnesses; these three assist the mind, and are therefore called mental factors (*caitta*).
Now, the characteristics of this defilement shall be explained.
The verse says:
Concealment and obstruction, establishment, leading forward, gathering, and fulfillment.
Because they consist of discernment, enjoyment, origination, bondage,
manifestation, and the fruit of suffering, these alone afflict the world;
the three, two, and seven types of defilements arise from false discrimination.
The Commentary states:
"Because of obscuration" means that because ignorance obscures the reality as it truly is and obstructs true vision.
"Because of establishment" means that because the karmic perfumations of the various formations are planted within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
"Because it leads" means that the appropriating consciousness (sopādāna-vijñāna) leads sentient beings to their place of birth.
"Because it encompasses" means that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) encompasses the individual existence of sentient beings.
"Because of fulfillment" means that the six internal bases cause sentient beings to possess complete physical integrity.
"Because of the threefold discrimination" means that contact is able to discriminate among the triad of sense organ, object, and consciousness, in accordance with the three types of feeling.
Regarding "because of experiencing": this means that by means of the link of sensation (*vedanā*), one experiences objects that are favorable, unfavorable, or neither.
Regarding "because of bringing about": this means that by the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the subsequent existence (*punarbhava*) projected by prior karma is brought into manifestation.
"Because of continuous binding" means that grasping causes consciousness to arise in continuous connection with the conditions of desire and so forth.
"Because of being present before one" means that by virtue of its power, it causes the various ripening fruits of previously performed karma to be manifested.
Regarding the phrase "because they are the fruit of suffering," this means that the nature of birth, aging, and death involves oppression, as they repay prior causes.
It is solely these twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) thus described that oppress the world, rendering it unstable and uneasy.
Regarding the three types of defilement: first, the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), which refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*);
second, the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), which refers to formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*);
third, the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*), which refers to the remaining members [of dependent origination].
Regarding the two types of defilement: first, causal defilement, which refers to afflictions and karma;
second, resultant defilement, which refers to the remaining members [of dependent origination].
Regarding the seven types of defilement, they refer to seven kinds of causes:
First is the cause of perversion, namely ignorance;
second is the cause of projection, namely volitional formations;
third is the cause of guidance, namely consciousness.
The fourth is the cause of appropriation, namely name-and-form and the six sense bases;
the fifth is the cause of experience, namely contact and feeling;
the sixth is the cause of origination, namely craving, grasping, and becoming.
The seven causes of aversion and fear are birth, old age, and death.
All these defilements arise and grow without exception through false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
This preceding section has generally revealed that false conceptualization possesses nine aspects:

1. The characteristic of existence; 2. The characteristic of non-existence; 3. The characteristic of specific characteristics; 4. The characteristic of inclusion; 5. The characteristic of the skillful means for entering non-existence; 6. The characteristic of differentiation; 7. The characteristic of synonyms; 8. The characteristic of origination; 9. The characteristic of affliction.
Having thus already clarified false discrimination, we shall now explain the emptiness of the objects of knowledge.
The verse says:
The various characteristics and alternative designations, The distinctions of meaning, and their establishment.
One should know that the two kinds of emptiness are briefly explained by means of these alone.
The Commentary says:
One should know that the emptiness of the grasped and the grasper is briefly explained only by these five characteristics and so forth.
What are the characteristics of the emptiness of the objects of knowledge?
The verse says:
Because it is neither dual nor existent or non-existent, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Neither different nor identical—this is explained as the characteristic of emptiness.
The Commentary says:
"Non-duality" means the absence of the grasped object and the grasping subject.
"Existence and non-existence" refers to the non-existence of the two types of grasping.
This reveals that emptiness has the absence of intrinsic nature as its very nature; therefore, this characteristic of emptiness is neither existent nor non-existent. Why is it not existent?
Because non-duality exists.
Why is it not non-existent?
Because duality does not exist.
This demonstrates that the characteristic of emptiness is neither existent nor non-existent.

This emptiness is neither different from nor identical to that false conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*); for if it were different, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) would be distinct from the phenomena themselves, which would contradict correct reasoning, as in the case of the nature of suffering and so forth.
If it were identical, it would follow that it is not the object of pure wisdom (*viśuddhajñāna*) and is not a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
This demonstrates that emptiness and false conceptualization are free from the characteristics of being either identical or different.
What are the alternative designations for the emptiness of the knowable?
The verse says:
In brief, the various synonyms for emptiness— namely, suchness, the limit of reality,
the signless, the ultimate nature, the dharma-realm, and so forth— should be understood.
The treatise says:
Briefly stated, there are these alternative formulations (*paryāya*) regarding emptiness.
How should the meaning of these alternative formulations be understood?
The verse says:
Because it is unchanging and non-erroneous, because it is the cessation of characteristics and the domain of noble wisdom,
and because it is the cause of all noble dharmas— these are the meanings of the synonyms, respectively.
The Commentary states:
That which is here described as the emptiness of the knowable is termed *tathatā* (suchness) in the sense of being unchanging.
It is called "true nature" (*bhūtatā*) because it is eternally such and lacks any transformation or alteration.
It is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi) in the sense of being non-erroneous, for it is not subject to the various inversions based on dependent phenomena.
It is called "signless" (animitta) in the sense of the cessation of signs, because within it all signs are forever severed.
It is called the "ultimate nature" (*paramārthatā*) in the sense of being the object of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), because it is the object traversed by the most supreme wisdom.
It is called the "dharma-sphere" (*dharmadhātu*) in the sense of being the cause of the noble dharmas, because all noble dharmas arise in dependence upon it.
In this context, "element" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "cause.
The meanings of "selflessness" and so forth should be understood according to reason.
How should the distinctions of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) be understood?
The verse says:
This defilement and purification arise from being with stains or without stains;
like water, the element of earth, gold, and space, they are held to be pure because they are inherently pure.
The treatise states:
There are briefly two types of differentiation regarding emptiness: first, defilement; second, purity.
This establishment of defilement and purity arises from the distinction of states; that is to say, the state with stains is called defiled, while the time of emerging from stains is called pure.
Although it is first defiled and subsequently becomes pure, there is no fault of transformation into impermanence.
Just as the element of water and so forth are freed from adventitious impurities, emptiness and purity are likewise not a transformation of intrinsic nature.

These distinctions of emptiness further comprise sixteen types, namely: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, great emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, non-dispersal emptiness, essential nature emptiness, characteristic emptiness, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-existence, and emptiness of the self-nature of non-existence.
How should the summarized meaning of these be understood?
The verse says:
The consumer and the consumed, This [latter] is the body upon which one dwells.
One who can see this according to reality perceives that the two sought-after purities are empty.
For the sake of constantly benefiting sentient beings, for not abandoning saṃsāra,
and for goodness that is inexhaustible, one contemplates these as empty.
To purify the spiritual lineage, to attain the primary and secondary marks,
and to purify all Buddha-dharmas, therefore the Bodhisattva contemplates emptiness.
The Commentary says:
The "emptiness that is able to consume" is spoken of in reliance upon the internal bases; it is internal emptiness.
The "emptiness that is consumed" is spoken of in reliance upon the external bases; it is external emptiness.
This "body as support" refers to the body that serves as the basis for both the consumer and the consumed; because this body is empty, it is called "internal-external emptiness.
The various receptacle worlds are said to be the "abode"; because their characteristics are vast, they are called "great," and because the abode itself is empty, it is called "great emptiness."
"One who is able to see this" refers to the wisdom that perceives the internal sense bases (*āyatana*) and so forth as empty.
Because the wisdom of emptiness itself is empty, it is called "the emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
"According to reality" (*yathābhūtam*) refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is the practice of suchness (*tathatā*).
The truth that is observed is itself emptiness; therefore, it is called the "emptiness of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Bodhisattvas practice in order to attain the two purities, which consist of all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) wholesome dharmas.
Because these two are empty, they are called the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).
Because one contemplates emptiness in order to constantly bring benefit to sentient beings, it is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
Birth and death are long and far-reaching, having neither beginning nor end; because one contemplates this as empty, it is called the "emptiness of the limitless" (anavara-śūnyatā).

One does not contemplate it as empty merely to quickly grow weary of and abandon it; rather, so as not to grow weary of and abandon this birth and death, one contemplates these limitless births and deaths as empty.

Because the virtues one has cultivated remain until the stage of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* without being discarded or scattered, as they contemplate emptiness, it is called "emptiness of non-dispersion" (*avikāra-śūnyatā*).
The lineage (*gotra*) of the noble ones exists as their own essential nature from the beginning; it is not something produced through cultivation, and is thus termed "original nature" (*prakṛti*).
Because the bodhisattva contemplates emptiness in order to swiftly attain purity, it is called "emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Because the bodhisattva contemplates emptiness in order to attain the marks and signs of a Great Being, it is called "emptiness of characteristics."

The Bodhisattva contemplates this emptiness in order to bring all Buddha-dharmas, such as the powers and the fearlessnesses, to complete purity; therefore, it is called the emptiness of all dharmas (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
These fourteen types of emptiness are established according to their specific distinctions.
In this context, what is it that is called "emptiness"?
The verse says:
The person and phenomena, Their real nature, are both non-existent.
Because of this absence of nature and presence of nature, two types of emptiness are established separately.
The Treatise says:
Because both the person (*pudgala*) and the true nature of phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent, it is called "emptiness of non-nature" (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).

This emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) is not a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); rather, because emptiness has non-existence as its very nature, it is called the "emptiness of the nature of non-existence" (*abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the previously mentioned "emptiness of the eater" (*bhoktṛ-śūnyatā*) and so forth, two further types of emptiness were established separately to manifest the characteristics of emptiness;

these latter two types of emptiness were established in their respective order to refute the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*), as well as the denial (*apavāda*) of emptiness.
Thus, the distinctions of emptiness have been revealed.
How should the meaning of this establishment be understood?
The verse says:
If this were not subject to defilement, everyone would be liberated of their own accord;
if this were not subject to purification, spiritual effort would bear no fruit.
The commentary says:
If all phenomena were empty such that no antidotes had arisen and there were no adventitious defilements, then all sentient beings would be naturally liberated without effort.
Conversely, if they were not purified even after the antidotes had arisen, then the exertion in seeking liberation would be fruitless.
This being so, the verse says:
Neither defiled nor non-defiled, Neither pure nor non-pure;
Because the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, It is defiled by adventitious dust.
The treatise says:
Why is it neither defiled nor non-defiled?
Because the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure.
What is neither pure nor impure?
It is so called because it is defiled by adventitious stains.
This is termed the establishment of the specific meanings of emptiness.
Prior to this, the meaning of emptiness generally comprises two aspects: characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and establishment (*vyavasthāna*).
Characteristics, in turn, are twofold: non-existence and existence.
The characteristic of the nature of emptiness consists in being free from existence and free from non-existence, and being free from difference and free from identity.
One should understand that "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhāpana*) refers to synonyms and so forth.
Chapter Two: Distinguishing Obstructions (*Āvaraṇavibhāga*). Having already distinguished their characteristics, the obstructions shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Complete or partial, intensified or balanced, regarding the adoption and rejection within birth and death—
these are said to be the two types of obstacles to the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
The commentary states:

The "obstacle consisting of all parts" refers to the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as they act as obstacles to all the dharmas within the lineage of the bodhisattvas.
The "obstacle consisting of one part" refers to the afflictive obstacle, as it acts as an obstacle to the dharmas within the lineages of the śrāvakas and others.
The obstacle of excess refers to those very [afflictions] characterized by greed and so forth.
The obstacle of equilibrium refers to those very [afflictions] characterized by equal proportions.

Because they obstruct the non-abiding nirvana attained by the bodhisattva lineage through the grasping and abandoning of birth and death, they are called "the obstacles regarding the grasping and abandoning of birth and death."
Thus, these five hindrances, according to their respective applications, are said to obstruct the two types of spiritual lineages: those of the bodhisattvas and the śrāvakas.
Furthermore, the verse says:
The characteristics of the nine kinds of afflictions Are the nine fetters, namely craving and the rest.
The first two [fetters] obstruct disenchantment and relinquishment; the remaining seven obstruct true vision.

That is to say, they can obstruct [the vision of] the view of a self, its object, cessation, the path, and the Jewels, as well as gain, honor, and so forth, because they prevent thorough knowledge through detachment.
The treatise states:
The characteristics of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are briefly of nine kinds, namely the nine kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*), such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The fetter of craving hinders revulsion, because by means of it one is unable to feel weary of or detach from favorable objects.
The fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) obstructs equanimity (*upekṣā*), because due to it one is unable to relinquish disagreeable objects.
The remaining seven fetters obstruct true vision (*bhūtadarśana*), as they respectively obstruct the seven thorough knowledges (*parijñā*).

That is to say, the fetter of pride can obstruct the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the view of a false self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); for when one is practicing the realization of the truths (*abhisamaya*), the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) arises both intermittently and continuously, and by its power, that [view] is not abandoned.

The fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) obstructs the full comprehension of the object of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), because through it one does not understand the aggregates of grasping (*upādāna-skandha*).

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) obstructs the full comprehension of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*); this is because the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) fear cessation, and because wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) denies cessation.
The fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) obstructs the thorough knowledge of the Truth of the Path, because it takes other phenomena to be pure.
The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) obstructs the thorough knowledge of the Three Jewels, because through it one does not have faith in or accept the qualities of the Three Jewels.
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) obstructs the thorough knowledge of gain, honor, and so forth, because through it one fails to perceive their faults.
The fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) obstructs the thorough knowledge of seclusion, because through it one is greedily attached to the requisites of life.
Furthermore, there are other obstacles that can obstruct the ten kinds of pure dharmas, such as the wholesome.
What are their characteristics?
The verse says:
Lacking application and improper basis, Unreasonable and failing to arise,
Failing to give rise to right reflection, And with the provisions not yet perfected;
Devoid of the spiritual lineage and virtuous friends, With a mind characterized by extreme weariness—
Furthermore, there is the deficiency in right practice, dwelling together with those who are base and evil;
the three types of inverted grossness, the lack of maturity in *prajñā*,
and the nature of innate grossness, as well as the nature of indolence and negligence.
Attached to existence and worldly wealth, with inferior mental dispositions,
lacking faith and resolute conviction, they contemplate the meaning according to the literal words;
they hold the Dharma in light esteem while valuing fame and profit, and lack compassion for sentient beings.
Lacking learning or possessing little learning, one does not cultivate sublime meditative concentration.
The commentary states:
These are called the obstacles to wholesome and other such dharmas.
What are the characteristics of the virtues and so forth that are obstructed?
The verse says:
Virtue, enlightenment, and gathering [of followers], Wisdom, and non-confusion are the objects of obstruction.
"Dedication, fearlessness, non-avarice, mastery, and so forth are called 'wholesome'.
The commentary states:
Regarding these ten kinds of pure dharmas, such as the wholesome and so on, who possesses how many of the previously mentioned obstacles?
The verse says:
Thus, for each of the ten [factors] beginning with the wholesome, there are three preceding obstacles.
The commentary says:
There are three obstacles to virtue: first, a lack of application; second, application in an improper object; and third, application that is not according to reason.
There are three obstacles to enlightenment: first, the non-arising of wholesome dharmas; second, the failure to give rise to correct reflection; and third, the incompleteness of the accumulations.

The arousal of the bodhicitta is termed "gathering" (parigraha); it has three obstacles: first, the absence of the spiritual lineage (gotra); second, the absence of virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra); and third, a nature of extreme weariness and fatigue.

One who possesses wisdom refers to a bodhisattva; regarding the realization of this nature, there are three kinds of obstacles: first, the absence of correct practice; second, dwelling together with those who are base; and third, dwelling together with those who are evil.
In this context, "vile" refers to those of a deluded nature; one who delights in destroying others is called "wicked.

There are three obstacles to non-confusion: first, the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of perversion; second, the state of having any remnant of the three obstacles, such as the afflictions (*kleśa*); and third, the lack of maturation of the wisdom that can ripen liberation.

The eradication of the obstacles to the [Buddha-]nature is called "unobstructedness. There are three such obstacles: first, innate heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*); second, the nature of indolence; and third, the nature of negligence.

Regarding dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), there are three obstacles that cause the mind to incline toward other things rather than toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment: first, attachment to various states of existence (*bhava*); second, attachment to material resources; and third, a base state of mind.
There are three obstacles to being free from fear: first, lack of faith and respect for the *pudgala*; second, lack of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding the Dharma;

and third, interpreting the meaning according to the literal expression. There are three obstacles to being free from stinginess: first, not honoring the True Dharma; second, honoring fame, gain, profit, and veneration; and third, lacking a mind of compassion toward sentient beings.

There are three obstacles to mastery that prevent one from attaining it: first, being deprived of hearing [the Dharma], because this engenders karma that results in the deprivation of the Dharma; second, hearing little; and third, not cultivating and refining superior samādhi.

Furthermore, regarding these various obstacles in relation to the ten [factors] such as the wholesome, there are ten types of "efficient causes" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) according to other meanings; one should understand that these names are applied based on those meanings.
The ten efficient causes are:
first, the cause of origination (*janana-kāraṇa*), such as the eye and so forth in relation to visual consciousness and so forth.
Second is the causal efficacy of abiding, as the four types of sustenance do for sentient beings.
Third is the causal efficacy of support, meaning that which can sustain, such as the receptacle world for the world of sentient beings.
Fourth is the causal efficacy of illumination, such as light in relation to various forms.
Fifth is the causal efficacy of transformation, such as fire in relation to that which is cooked.
Sixth is the causal efficacy of separation, such as a sickle in relation to that which is cut.
Seventh is the productive cause as transformation (*pariṇāma-kāraka*), such as goldsmiths and others transforming gold and so forth into rings, bracelets, and the like.
Eighth is the productive cause as conviction (*adhimukti-kāraka*), such as smoke and so forth with respect to fire and so forth.
Ninth is the manifesting efficient cause (*abhivyakti-kāraka*), such as the reason (*hetu*) in relation to the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Tenth is the attaining efficient cause (*prāpti-kāraka*), such as the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) in relation to Nirvāṇa and so forth.
Based on this meaning, a verse is spoken:
There are ten kinds of causal efficiency (*kāraṇa*): namely, production, maintenance, support, illumination, transformation, separation, modification, conviction, manifestation, and attainment;
these are like consciousness, a cause, food, the earth, a lamp, fire, a sickle, and craftsmanship.
"Smoke, causes, the noble path, and so forth, act upon consciousness and the like.
It should be understood that the same applies to the obstructions to the wholesome and so on.
First, there is the obstruction to arising; this refers to the wholesome, because all wholesome dharmas ought to arise.
Second is the obstacle to abiding securely, which refers to [the obstacle] regarding enlightenment, because Great Enlightenment is immovable.
Third is the obstacle to sustaining, which refers to [the obstacle] regarding the gathering [of disciples], because the bodhicitta is able to sustain them.
Fourth is the obstacle to clear comprehension, which refers to wisdom; because one possesses the nature of wisdom, one ought to clearly comprehend.
Fifth is the obstacle of transformation and destruction, which refers to non-confusion; because the overturning and cessation of delusion is termed "transformation and destruction."
Sixth is the obstacle of separation, which refers to being unobstructed, because it is the dissociation from obstacles.
Seventh is the obstacle of transformation, which refers to dedication, because it has the characteristic of transforming [the roots of virtue] into the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Eighth is the obstacle to resolute belief (*adhimukti*), which refers to fear regarding that which is not to be feared, because one who lacks resolute belief experiences dread.
Ninth is the obstacle to manifesting, which refers to stinginess regarding the Dharma; for one who is not stingy with the Dharma manifests it for the sake of others.
The tenth is the obstacle to attainment (*prāpti-vibandha*), meaning that regarding one's own mastery, this constitutes the characteristic of being able to attain mastery.

As for the sequential meaning of the ten dharmas thus obstructed: it means that one who wishes to realize unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*) must first give rise to superior roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*); because they are sustained by the power of these superior roots of goodness, one will necessarily abide in unsurpassed enlightenment.
In order to cause one's roots of goodness to increase, one should next give rise to the mind of great enlightenment (bodhicitta); this bodhicitta serves as the basis for the nature of a bodhisattva.

In this way, because a bodhisattva is sustained by the power of having already generated the mind of great enlightenment and superior roots of goodness, they sever all forms of confusion and error, giving rise to non-confusion and non-error.
Because there is no delusion within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one subsequently abandons all hindrances during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Once the hindrances have been abandoned, one dedicates all roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Sustained by the power of dedication, one becomes free from fear regarding the profound and vast Dharma.
Being without fear, one perceives the supreme qualities within that Dharma and is able to extensively proclaim and reveal it to others.

Because the Bodhisattva is sustained by the power of such various merits, they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment and attain mastery over all phenomena; these are called the ten meanings in their proper sequence, beginning with "skillful" (*kuśala*).

Although wholesome factors such as these are indeed the constituents of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), and the qualities of the stages (*bhūmi*), they differ in their general and specific aspects; now, one should clarify the distinctions among the various obstacles to those factors conducive to enlightenment and so forth.
The verse says:
Regarding the factors of enlightenment, the perfections, and the stages, one should know that there are distinct obstacles.
The commentary says:
Furthermore, regarding the virtues of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*) across the various stages, each has its own specific obstacle.
Concerning the specific obstacles to the factors of enlightenment, the verse says:
"Ineptitude regarding the objective, Laziness, and the two types of diminished concentration."
One does not cultivate a weak or inferior nature, but perceives the faults of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
The commentary states:
regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there is the obstacle of being unskilled in all phenomena (*vastu*).
Regarding the four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*), there is the obstacle of laziness.

Regarding the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), there are obstacles consisting of the deficiency of two factors concerning meditative concentration (*samādhi*): first, the deficiency of any one among desire, effort, mind, or investigation for its perfection; second, the deficiency of any one among the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) during cultivation.
Regarding the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), there is the obstacle of not having planted the supreme wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in their full perfection.
Regarding the five powers (*pañcabala*), there is the obstacle of weakness; that is, the very same five faculties, when mixed with obstacles, possess a state of weakness.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, there is the obstacle of the fault of views, because this is what is revealed by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding the eight branches of the noble path, there is the obstacle of the fault of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*), because this is what is revealed by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding the specific obstacles to the perfections (pāramitās), the verse says:
Obstacles to wealth and status, to the happy realms, To not abandoning sentient beings, and to the loss of virtues or the increase of faults;
[Obstacles] to causing [beings] to enter [the path], and to liberation.
It obstructs various virtues such as giving; it is inexhaustible and uninterrupted;
it ensures the certainty of performed virtues; and it brings to maturity the enjoyment of the Dharma.
The commentary says:
This explains the obstacles to the fruits obtained from the ten *pāramitās*, thereby revealing the obstacles to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those ten *pāramitās*.
Specifically, regarding the *dāna-pāramitā*, it speaks of the obstacle of wealth and power;
regarding the *śīla-pāramitā*, it speaks of the obstacle to the higher realms (*sugati*).
Regarding the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), it is said that there is the obstacle of not relinquishing sentient beings;
regarding the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā), it is said that there is the obstacle of diminishing faults and increasing virtues;
regarding the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā), it is said that there is the obstacle of causing those to be converted to enter the Dharma.
Regarding the *prajñāpāramitā*, it speaks of the obstacle to liberation;

regarding the *upāyakauśalyapāramitā*, it speaks of the obstacle to the inexhaustibility of virtuous qualities such as giving, because through dedication toward unsurpassed enlightenment, these virtues like giving are rendered inexhaustible;

regarding the *praṇidhānapāramitā*, it speaks of the obstacle to the uninterrupted succession of virtue throughout all births, because by the power of great vows, one is sustained so that births favorable to virtuous dharmas may occur.

Regarding the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), it is said that there is an obstacle to attaining certainty regarding the wholesome deeds one performs; this is because those obstacles can be suppressed by the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*) and the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*), rather than being suppressed by them [independently].

Regarding the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*), it is said that there is an obstacle to the maturation of the enjoyment of the Dharma for oneself and others, because one does not realize the meaning according to how it was heard.
Regarding the specific obstacles to the qualities of the stages (*bhūmi*), the verse says:
Pervasive and supreme, The flow of excellence and non-appropriation,
Continuity without differentiation, And the absence of both defilement and purification.
The various dharmas are without distinction, Neither increasing nor decreasing, and free from conceptualization; These are the meanings of the four masteries.
Regarding these ten dharma realms, There exists non-afflicted ignorance.
They obstruct the merits of the ten stages; therefore, they are called the ten obstructions.
The treatise says:

Within the ten dharma-spheres, such as the all-pervading and so forth, there exists the obstruction of non-defiled ignorance; these are established as the obstructions to the ten stages, corresponding respectively to the merits of those ten stages.

That which is called the "meaning of universal pervasion" refers to the dharma-realm realized in the first stage; by penetrating this, one realizes the equality of the dharma-nature of oneself and others.
That which is called the "meaning of supremacy" refers to the dharma-realm realized in the second stage; by penetrating this, one reflects:
"Therefore, I shall now universally cultivate and purify all practices associated with renunciation"; this constitutes the diligent cultivation of practices associated with renunciation.

The dharma-realm realized in the third stage is called the "meaning of the supreme outflow. By penetrating this, one knows that the teachings heard are the most excellent outflow of the pure dharma-realm; for the sake of seeking this Dharma, even if there were a pit of fire as vast as a trichiliocosm, one would cast oneself into it to obtain it without regarding it as difficult.
The dharma-realm realized in the fourth stage is called the meaning of non-appropriation; by penetrating this, even attachment to the Dharma is completely transformed and extinguished.
The dharma-realm realized in the fifth stage is called the meaning of the non-differentiation of continuity; by penetrating this, one attains the pure mind of the tenfold equality of intention.

The dharma-realm realized in the sixth stage is called "the meaning of neither defilement nor purification"; by penetrating this, one knows that dependently originated phenomena are neither defiled nor pure.

The dharma-realm realized in the seventh stage is called "the meaning of the non-differentiation of various dharmas. By penetrating this, one knows that dharmas are signless and does not engage with the various characteristics of dharmas such as the sūtras and so forth.

The dharma-realm realized in the eighth stage is called the meaning of neither increasing nor decreasing; by penetrating this, one fully realizes the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and among all pure and defiled phenomena, one does not perceive even a single phenomenon as increasing or decreasing.
There are four masteries:
first, mastery over non-conceptuality; second, mastery over the pure land; third, mastery over wisdom; and fourth, mastery over karma.
The dharma-realm serves as the basis for these four types, which is termed the meaning of being the support for the four masteries.
In the eighth stage, one is able to penetrate only the meaning of the basis for the first two masteries.

In the ninth stage, one is also able to penetrate the meaning of the basis for mastery over knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā*), because of the perfect realization of the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
In the tenth stage, one further attains mastery over karma, in the sense that one can manifest various deeds for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings according to one's wish.
A summary verse states:
The various afflictions And the various cognitive obscurations have already been explained.
Because these two are admitted to be exhausted, all obstacles are liberated.
The Commentary says:
Since these two encompass all obstacles, it is admitted that when they are exhausted, one is liberated from all obstacles.
The general meaning of the preceding hindrances consists of eleven types:
first, the extensive hindrance, which refers to the complete hindrance;
second, the limited hindrance, which refers to the partial hindrance.
Third is the obstacle to preparatory application (*prayoga*), namely the obstacle of excessive intensity.
Fourth is the obstacle to attainment (*prāpti*), namely the obstacle of equanimity.
Fifth is the obstacle to excellence (*viśeṣa*), namely the obstacle of grasping at and abandoning birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Sixth is the obstacle to correct application (*samyak-prayoga*), which refers to the nine obstacles consisting of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Seventh is the causal obstacle (*hetu-āvaraṇa*), which refers to the obstacles to the ten types of efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) regarding the wholesome and so forth.
Eighth is the obstacle to entering reality (*tattva-praveśa*), which refers to the obstacles to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
Ninth is the obstacle to supreme purity, which refers to the obstacles to the *pāramitās*.
Tenth is the obstacle to these specific attainments, which refers to the obstacles to the ten stages (*bhūmis*).
Eleventh is the obstacle of inclusion, which refers to a summary of the two types of obstacles.
