Chapter Three: Distinguishing Reality. Having already distinguished its obstacles, reality shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Reality is truly of ten kinds, namely: the fundamental and its characteristics, non-perversion, cause and effect, as well as coarse and subtle reality.
The ten skillful realities— those that are universally established, those within the range of pure cognition, those involving appropriation,
and those involving differentiation— are all for the purpose of eliminating the view of a self.
The Commentary says:

One should know that there are exactly ten kinds of reality: first, fundamental reality; second, reality of characteristics; third, reality free from error; fourth, reality of cause and effect; fifth, reality of the coarse and the subtle; sixth, reality of established consensus; seventh, reality of the sphere of pure practice; eighth, reality of inclusion; ninth, reality of differentiation; and tenth, reality of skillfulness.
These further consist of ten types, intended for the removal of the ten views of self. The ten types of skillfulness are: first, skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*);

second, skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu*); third, skillfulness regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*); fourth, skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); fifth, skillfulness regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*); sixth, skillfulness regarding the faculties (*indriya*); seventh, skillfulness regarding the time periods (*adhvan*); eighth, skillfulness regarding the truths (*satya*); ninth, skillfulness regarding the vehicles (*yāna*); and tenth, skillfulness regarding conditioned and unconditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtāsaṃskṛta-dharma*).
In this context, what is the fundamental reality?
It refers to the three natures: first, the imagined nature; second, the dependent nature; and third, the perfected nature, because it is based upon these that the other realities are established.
Among these three natures thus explained, which meaning is accepted as being ultimately real?
The verse says:
Among the three natures, it is accepted that one is eternally non-existent.
One exists but is not real; one exists as neither real nor unreal.
The commentary states:
Regarding these three natures (*trisvabhāva*):
The thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa) is eternally non-existent;
it is only eternally non-existent that is accepted as the reality within this nature, because it is free from inversion.
The dependent nature (paratantra-lakṣaṇa) exists but is not real.
Only that which is "mere existence" (yod pa tsam) is accepted as real within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it possesses a nature of delusion.
Furthermore, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) also has both "existence" and "non-existence.
Only that which is "mere non-existence" (med pa tsam) is accepted as real within this nature, because it possesses the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
What is the reality of characteristics?
The verse says:
Regarding phenomena, the person, and that which is grasped and the grasper—
Within the nature of existence and non-existence, there are views of superimposition and denial;
by knowing this, one does not waver—this is called the characteristic of reality.
The Commentary says:

Regarding all phenomena, the views of superimposition and denial concerning persons—if one knows this, such views no longer arise—this is the true characteristic of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).

Regarding all views of superimposition and denial within the phenomena of the grasped and the grasper, if one knows this [nature], they no longer arise; this is called the true characteristic of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Regarding existence and non-existence, if one knows those views of superimposition and denial such that they no longer arise, this is called the true characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Because this is non-erroneous regarding the fundamental characteristic of reality, it is called the "reality of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇatattva*).
The "reality of non-error" refers to impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness; by means of these, one remedies the four inversions such as permanence and so forth.
How should one understand that these [characteristics] such as impermanence are established based upon that fundamental reality?
The verse says:
Non-existence, arising and ceasing, And defilement and purity—these are the three types of impermanence.
The grasped object, the thing-in-itself, and their conjunction—these are the three kinds of suffering;
emptiness likewise has three kinds: namely, non-existence, difference, and intrinsic nature;
signlessness, the absence of difference, and the absence of self-nature—these are the three kinds of selflessness.
The four and three types, respectively, are based on the fundamental reality.
The treatise says:

Regarding the three types of impermanence, first is impermanence as the absence of intrinsic nature, which refers to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); this is because it is eternally non-existent.
Second is impermanence as arising and ceasing, which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it has origination and extinction;
third is impermanence as defilement and purification, which refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because its states undergo transformation.

Regarding the three kinds of suffering: first, the suffering of the grasped (*grāhya-duḥkha*), which refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva*, because it is that which is grasped by the clinging to a person (*pudgala*) and to phenomena (*dharma*);
second, the suffering of phenomenal characteristics (*vastu-lakṣaṇa-duḥkha*), which refers to the *paratantra-svabhāva*, because it possesses the characteristics of the three types of suffering;
third, the suffering of conjunction (*saṃyoga-duḥkha*), which refers to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*, because it is conjoined with the characteristics of suffering.

There are three kinds of emptiness: first, emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*), which refers to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); since this lacks any rational basis that could be said to exist, it is called empty because it does not exist.

Second, emptiness of other-nature (*anya-bhāva-śūnyatā*), which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); as it is falsely grasped, it does not exist in that manner, yet it is not entirely non-existent in every respect.

Third, emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), which refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); for its self-nature is that which is revealed by the two [preceding] forms of emptiness.

Regarding the three kinds of selflessness (*anātman*): first, selflessness as the absence of characteristics (*animitta-anātman*), which refers to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Because these characteristics are fundamentally non-existent, they are called "without characteristics," and this very absence of characteristics is termed selflessness.

Second, selflessness as distinct characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa-anātman*), which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Although these characteristics exist, they do not exist in the manner of the thoroughly imagined nature; thus, they are called "distinct characteristics," and this very distinct characteristic is termed selflessness.

Third, selflessness as intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-anātman*), which refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). That which is revealed by the absence of self is taken as its intrinsic characteristic, and this very intrinsic characteristic is termed selflessness.

Regarding these four aspects thus described—impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—they are each divided into three types according to their respective fundamental realities in their sequential order; one should understand that each of the four has three types as previously explained.
The reality of cause and effect refers to the Four Noble Truths. How do these depend upon fundamental reality?
The verse says:
The three characteristics of suffering have already been explained; likewise, there are three types of origin.
Namely: habitual tendencies, origination, and characteristics not yet dissociated;
intrinsic nature, the two non-arisings, defilement, tranquility, and the two types of cessation.
"Thorough knowledge, permanent abandonment, and the realization of the truths of the three paths.
The commentary states:
There are three aspects to the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya), namely the four characteristics such as impermanence, each having three aspects, as previously explained.

The three aspects of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) are: first, the origination of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which refers to the habitual tendencies of clinging to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
second, the origination of co-emergence (*samutthāna*), which refers to karma and afflictions (*kleśa*);
and third, the origination of non-separation from fetters (*avisamyoga*), which refers to suchness (*tathatā*) that has not yet been freed from obstructions.
The three aspects of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) are: first, cessation by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirodha*), meaning that intrinsic nature does not arise;
second, cessation of the two grasps (*dvaya-grāha-nirodha*), meaning that the grasped object and the grasping subject do not arise;

and third, cessation of original nature (*prakṛti-nirodha*), which refers to the two—namely, the quiescence of defilements (*praśama*) and suchness (*tathatā*), i.e., analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and true suchness (*tathatā*).
The Truth of the Path consists of three aspects: first, the path of thorough knowledge; second, the path of perpetual abandonment; and third, the path of realization.

It should be understood that herein, with respect to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature), there is only thorough knowledge; with respect to the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature), there is both thorough knowledge and perpetual abandonment; and with respect to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature), there is both thorough knowledge and realization. Thus, the Truth of the Path is established based on these three.
The coarse and the subtle reality refer to the conventional and ultimate truths.
How do these depend upon fundamental reality?
The verse says:
One should know that conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is differentiated into three types:
namely, the nominal (prajñapti), the conditioned (pravṛtti), and the manifest (abhivyakti); these correspond respectively to the three fundamental [truths].
The ultimate truth is also threefold: namely, the object, attainment, and correct practice;
based on the single fundamental [nature], it is unchanging, non-erroneous, and twofold perfection.
The treatise states:
There are three types of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): first, the conventional of designation (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti*); second, the conventional of practice (*pracāra-saṃvṛti*);
and third, the conventional of manifestation (*pratipatti-saṃvṛti*). These three conventions are established, respectively, based upon the three fundamental realities (*mūla-tattva*).

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is also threefold: first, the ultimate as object (*artha-paramārtha*), which refers to suchness (*tathatā*), because it is called the ultimate as it is the object of supreme wisdom;
second, the ultimate as attainment (*prāpti-paramārtha*), which refers to nirvāṇa, because this is both a supreme fruit and a meaningful benefit;
third, the ultimate as correct practice (*pratipatti-paramārtha*), which refers to the noble path (*āryamārga*), because it takes the supreme dharma as its object.
These three ultimate realities (paramārtha) should be understood as being established solely based on the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) among the three fundamental natures.
This perfected nature is, in general, of two kinds, due to the distinction between the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and the conditioned (saṃskṛta).
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) encompasses suchness (*tathatā*) and nirvāṇa; because it is devoid of change, it is called the "perfectly established" (*pariniṣpanna*).
The conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) encompasses all noble paths (*āryamārga*); because it is non-erroneous regarding its objects, it is also called the "perfectly established."
There are, in brief, two kinds of thoroughly established reality: first, the thoroughly established reality of worldly consensus; second, the thoroughly established reality of reasoning.
How are these two established based upon that fundamental reality?
The verse says:
That which is established by worldly consensus relies on one; that which is established by reason relies on three.
The commentary says:

If a thing is established by common worldly consensus, apprehended by a cognitive awareness that has entered into it through habitual practice, and all the world collectively maintains that this thing is earth and not fire, or color and not sound, and so forth, this is called the "truth universally established in the world" (*lokaprasiddhatattva*).
Among these three fundamental realities, this is established solely based on the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

If there is one who is rational, wise, intelligent, and capable of analytical investigation, who establishes and posits it by relying on the principles of proof through the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this is called the reality established by reasoning (*yukti-prasiddha-tattva*).
This is established based on the three fundamental realities.

The reality of the purified sphere of practice is also briefly of two kinds: first, the reality of the sphere of practice for wisdom purified of the afflictive obscurations; second, the reality of the sphere of practice for wisdom purified of the cognitive obscurations.
How are these two established based upon that fundamental reality?
The verse says:
The objects of pure practice are of two kinds, based upon one: the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The Commentary states:

The two obstacles—afflictive and cognitive—and the reality that is the object of purified wisdom, are established solely based on the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) among the three fundamental realities, because the other two [realities] are not the objects of this purified wisdom.

How should one understand that the aspects (*lakṣaṇa*), names (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) are subsumed within the three fundamental realities?
The verse says:
Names are the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); Aspects and conceptualization are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Suchness and correct cognition are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The treatise states:

"The five categories, beginning with characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), are subsumed, as appropriate, within the three fundamental natures. That is to say, names are subsumed under the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); characteristics and conceptualization are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and suchness and correct cognition are subsumed under the perfected nature."
The reality of differentiation is, in brief, of seven kinds:

first, the reality of phenomenal evolution; second, the reality of the true nature of phenomena; third, the reality of representation-only; fourth, the reality of formal establishment; fifth, the reality of erroneous practice; sixth, the reality of purification; and seventh, the reality of correct practice.
How should one understand that these seven realities are established based upon the three fundamental realities?
The verse says:
"Evolution and establishment, And erroneous practice depend on the first two."
The true nature (*tathatā*), consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), and purity; Right practice (*samyakpratipatti*) relies on the latter one.
The Commentary says:

The seven [topics], beginning with "evolution" (*pravṛtti*), are subsumed, as appropriate, within the three fundamental types of reality (*tattva*). That is to say, evolution, establishment (*vyavasthāna*), and wrong practice (*mithyāpratipatti*) rely upon the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*) natures among the fundamentals. True nature, consciousness-only, purity, and right practice rely upon the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) nature among the fundamentals.
Skillful reality refers to the ten types [of selflessness] taught as an antidote to the ten views of self.
How do the ten views of self arise with respect to the aggregates and so forth?
The verse says:
Regarding the aggregates and so forth, the view of self consists of grasping [them] as one,
as cause, as enjoyer, as agent, as that which acts with sovereignty, as supreme, and as permanent.
The basis for affliction and purification, the nature of the observer, and the nature of the one who is bound or liberated.

The commentary states: Regarding the ten phenomena beginning with the aggregates (*skandha*), ten kinds of views of a self arise: first, the adherence to a single nature; second, the adherence to the nature of a cause; third, the adherence to the nature of an experiencer; fourth, the adherence to the nature of an agent; fifth, the adherence to the nature of one who acts with sovereignty; sixth, the adherence to the nature of a dominant factor; seventh, the adherence to permanence; eighth, the adherence to the nature of the basis for affliction and purification; ninth, the adherence to the nature of a practitioner; and tenth, the adherence to the nature of one who is bound or liberated.
To eliminate these views, one cultivates the ten types of skillfulness.
How are these ten kinds of skillful reality established based on the three fundamental realities?
It is because the ten categories, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), are all subsumed within the three fundamental natures (*svabhāva*).
How are these subsumed within the three natures?
The verse says:
"This [nature] is the grasped and the conceptualized; the meaning of dharmatā resides therein."
The treatise states:
Each of these ten categories, such as the aggregates and so forth, possesses three meanings.

To begin with, regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), there are three meanings: first, the meaning of form as that which is grasped (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which refers to the imagined nature of form.

Second is matter in the sense of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-artha-rūpa*), which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of matter, because it is conceptually constructed as matter therein;
third is matter in the sense of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-artha-rūpa*), which refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of matter.

Just as these three meanings exist within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), one should understand accordingly that each of the other four aggregates—feeling and so forth—and each of the nine factors, such as the elements (*dhātu*), likewise possesses these three meanings.

Thus, because the aggregates and so forth are distinguished by these three meanings, there is nothing that is not subsumed within those three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Therefore, it should be known that the ten types of expertise regarding reality (*daśa-vidyā-sthāna-tattva*) are all established based upon the three fundamental realities.

Thus, although it has been stated that one cultivates skill in the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as an antidote to the ten kinds of views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the specific meanings of these aggregates and so forth have not yet been explained.
For now, how should the meaning of the first [aggregate], the aggregate, be understood?
The verse says:
Because they are not one, because they are a collective summary, and because of the meaning of "divided portions," they are called *skandhas*.
The commentary says:
One should know that the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) is, in brief, threefold:
first, the sense of "not one," as stated in the sūtra:
"Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near."
2. The meaning of general summary, as stated in the sūtra:
"All these, briefly condensed, form a single aggregate.
3. The meaning of sectional division, as stated in the sūtra:

The aggregates of form and so forth are so named because the specific characteristics of form and the others are established individually; thus, the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) is established through the sense of a "collection" (rāśi).
Furthermore, we observe in the world that the term "aggregate" is used in the sense of a collection.
The meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*) has already been explained; what is the meaning of the elements (*dhātu*)?
The verse says:
The grasper, the grasped, and that which grasps— In the sense of being seeds, they are called "elements."
The treatise states:
The meaning of the seeds of the apprehending subject refers to the six internal bases, such as the eye and so forth.
The meaning of the seeds of the apprehended object refers to the six external bases, such as form and so forth.
That which takes up the sense of "seed" refers to the six consciousness-elements, beginning with eye-consciousness.
The meaning of the *dhātus* has already been explained; what is the meaning of the *āyatanas*?
The verse says:
The sense of being the "gate of utilization" for that which is able to receive [objects] and the objects to be cognized is called an *āyatana* (base).
The treatise says:
Herein, the sense of being the gate of utilization for that which is able to receive refers to the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*).
If the meaning of the objects of experience that are cognized is the sense of "basis" (*āyatana*), these are the six external bases.
Having explained the meaning of the bases, what is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
The verse says:
The meaning of dependent origination involves no increase or decrease regarding cause, effect, and function.
The treatise states:
When there is neither superimposition nor denial with respect to cause, effect, and function, this is the meaning of dependent origination.
It should be understood that herein, "superimposing a cause" refers to the adherence to the existence of an unequal cause for formations and so forth;
"denying a cause" refers to the adherence to their being causeless;
and "superimposing a result" refers to the adherence to the arising of formations and so forth from conditions such as ignorance while maintaining the notion of a self.
The diminution of the result consists in maintaining that ignorance and so forth have no results such as volitional formations and so forth.
The exaggeration of function consists in maintaining that ignorance and so forth have a distinct causal efficacy in producing volitional formations and so forth.
Regarding the depreciation of function: this refers to the adherence that ignorance and the other factors possess no capacity whatsoever for the production of the formations and so forth.
If one is free from these three types of adherence to increase and decrease, it should be known that such a person is skilled in dependent origination.
The meaning of dependent origination has already been explained. What is the meaning of "the possible" (*sthāna*) and "the impossible" (*asthāna*)?
The verse says:
Regarding the undesirable, the desirable, purity, simultaneous arising, and the sovereign lord;
"Attainment and practice lack sovereignty; this is the meaning of the possible and the impossible.
The commentary states:
The meaning of the possible and the impossible should be understood through its characteristics, which briefly consist of seven kinds of lack of sovereignty.
First, there is lack of mastery over what is undesirable: that is, by means of unwholesome conduct, one falls into the miserable realms despite having no desire to do so.
Second, there is lack of mastery over what is desirable: that is, by means of sublime conduct, one ascends to the happy realms despite having no desire to do so.

Third, one lacks mastery over purification; that is, by not abandoning the five hindrances and not cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, one is certain to be unable to bring an end to suffering.
Fourth, there is no mastery over co-arising, meaning that two Tathāgatas or two wheel-turning kings do not appear simultaneously in a single world-system.
Fifth, there is no mastery over superior status, meaning that a woman does not become a wheel-turning king, and so forth.
Sixth is the lack of mastery over realization, meaning that women do not realize the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Seventh is the lack of mastery over manifestation, meaning that those who have seen the truths will certainly not manifest acts such as taking life.

Ordinary worldlings may still manifest such [unwholesome states]; these are explained in detail in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*. One should understand, according to this, what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
Having thus explained the meaning of possibility and impossibility, what is the meaning of the faculties (*indriya*)?
The verse says:
The faculties have predominance over grasping, abiding, continuity, function, and the two purities.
The commentary says:

The twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) are established by way of their predominance (*ādhipatya*) with respect to six matters: namely, the six faculties beginning with the eye possess predominance with respect to the apprehension of objects; the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) possesses predominance with respect to the maintenance of the continuity of a single lifetime; the two sexual faculties possess predominance with respect to the continuation of the family lineage; the five faculties beginning with pleasure possess predominance with respect to the experience of the results of wholesome and unwholesome karma; the five worldly faculties beginning with faith possess predominance with respect to mundane purification; and the supramundane faculties beginning with "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) possess predominance with respect to supramundane purification.
The meaning of the faculties (*indriya*) has already been explained. What is the meaning of "time" (*adhvan*)?
The verse says:
"The meaning of time should be understood as the causal function of what has already occurred and what has not yet occurred."
The treatise says:
One should know that the distinction of the three time periods according to their respective applications concerns whether cause and fruit have already been experienced or not yet experienced.
That is to say, when both cause and fruit have already been experienced, this is the meaning of the past;
If neither the cause nor the effect has yet been experienced, this is the meaning of the future;
if the cause has already been experienced but the effect has not yet been experienced, this is the meaning of the present.
The meaning of the world has already been explained; what is the meaning of the truths?
The verse says:
Suffering and the provisions for suffering, as well as the formative forces that cause them.
"The two types of pacification as antidotes—this is the meaning of 'truth' (satya) that should be known.
The treatise says:
"One should know that 'truths' refers to the Four Noble Truths."
The first is the Noble Truth of Suffering, which refers to all sensations (*vedanā*) and the requisites for sensation.
As it is stated in the Sūtras: "Whatever is felt, all that is suffering."
The aggregate of feeling refers to those phenomena conducive to feeling.
The second noble truth, the truth of origination, refers to those formative forces which are the causes of that very suffering.
The third noble truth, the truth of cessation, refers to the ultimate pacification of the former two types.
The four noble truths refer to suffering, its origin, and the path that serves as their antidote.
Having explained the meaning of "truth" (*satya*), what is the meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*)?
The verse says:
Through merits and faults, as well as non-conceptual wisdom,
and by means of the dependent nature for one's own liberation— this is the meaning of the vehicle that should be understood.
The treatise says:
One should know that "vehicles" refers to the three vehicles, the meaning of which shall be explained here as appropriate.
If one gives rise to this wisdom by hearing from others about the virtues of nirvāṇa and the faults of saṃsāra, and attains liberation through this wisdom, this is the Śrāvaka vehicle.

The Pratyekabuddhayāna consists of those who, without hearing from others about the virtues of nirvāṇa or the faults of saṃsāra, spontaneously give rise to this wisdom, and by means of this wisdom, attain liberation.
If non-conceptual wisdom arises spontaneously, and one attains liberation by means of this wisdom, it is called the Unsurpassed Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).
Having explained the meaning of "vehicle," what is the meaning of conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena?
The verse says:
The meanings of the conditioned and the unconditioned are defined as the conventional, the causal,
and the characteristic.
"Whether it be tranquility, or the object observed therein.
The treatise says:
It should be understood that "designation" (*prajñapti*) herein refers to names and so forth;
The "cause" refers to the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as comprised of seeds;

the "characteristic" refers to the environment, the body, and the objects of enjoyment, as well as the mental faculty (manas), the grasping, and the discursive thought subsumed under the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna);
the "mental faculty" refers to the consciousness whose nature is constant reflection.
"Apprehension" refers to the five consciousnesses, because they apprehend present objects;
"reflection" is the sixth mental consciousness, because it is able to discern all objects.
Thus, whether they be designations, causes, characteristics, or associated mental factors, these are collectively termed "conditioned."
"Quiescence" refers to both the cessation that is realized and the path that realizes it, because they are capable of bringing about quiescence.
"The object of observation" for that [quiescence] refers to suchness itself, as it is the objective referent of the path of quiescence.
Thus, what has been explained—both the various states of tranquility and the objects of observation—is collectively termed the "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).

It should be understood that within this context, the correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) arising from taking the ten objects such as the aggregates (*skandha*) as its focal point is called "skillfulness regarding the aggregates" (*skandha-kauśalya*), and so forth.
The general meaning of reality is briefly twofold: namely, the reality that reveals and the reality that is revealed.
The reality that reveals refers to the first three fundamental [realities], as they are able to reveal the others.
The reality that is manifested consists of the latter nine types, because they are what is revealed by the first fundamental [reality].
As for these nine manifestations: first, the reality manifested as being free from overweening pride;
second, the reality manifested as the remedy for perversions.
Third, the reality manifested by the renunciation of the Śrāvaka-yāna;
fourth, the reality manifested by the renunciation of the Mahāyāna, because the coarse [teachings] can bring about maturation while the subtle can bring about liberation;
fifth, the reality manifested by the ability to subdue the arguments of others, because one subdues others by employing analogies to guide them through reasoning.
Sixth, the reality revealed by the manifest Great Vehicle;
seventh, the reality revealed by all aspects of the knowable;
eighth, the reality revealed by the non-erroneous *tathatā*.
The ninth [topic] concerns the reality revealed by all secrets regarding the objects of the grasping at a self.

Chapter Four: Distinguishing the Cultivation of Antidotes. Having already distinguished reality, we shall now distinguish the cultivation of the various antidotes, which is the cultivation of all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Among these, one should first explain the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
The verse says:
Because of the cause of craving for the heavy residues (dausthulya), and because there is no delusion regarding the object of the self (ātman).
To enter the Four Noble Truths, one should know that the foundations of mindfulness are cultivated.
The commentary states:
Since the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) are manifested through the body, one enters the Noble Truth of Suffering by observing this.

Because the body has the characteristic of being accompanied by various states of heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), and because these states of heaviness are themselves the nature of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), the Noble Ones perceive all that is contaminated (*sāsrava*) as suffering.
Since all contaminated feelings are said to be the cause of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one observes them as entering into the Noble Truth of the Origin (*samudaya-satya*).

The mind is the objective basis for the grasping of a self; therefore, by investigating it, one enters the Noble Truth of Cessation, because through this [investigation], one becomes free from the fear that the self will be annihilated.
By investigating phenomena (*dharma*), one enters the Noble Truth of the Path, becoming free from delusion regarding defiled and purified phenomena.
Therefore, in order to enter into the principle of the Four Noble Truths, the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) was taught first.
Having already explained the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, the cultivation of the right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Having thoroughly understood the obstacles and their remedies, as well as all their various distinctions,
one diligently cultivates the four right efforts for the sake of abandoning [the former] and cultivating [the latter].
The Commentary states:
Having previously cultivated the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one has already been able to fully know the distinctions between all categories of obstacles and their remedies.
Now, in order to abandon the obstructive factors that are to be countered and to cultivate the path that serves as the remedy, one diligently practices the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
As it has been said: "For the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having explained the cultivation of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), one should now explain the cultivation of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
The verse says:
Relying on the state of fitness and stability, for the sake of accomplishing all tasks,
one eliminates the five faults and diligently cultivates the eight formative forces of abandonment.
The treatise says:

Based on the previously cultivated diligence of abandoning accumulation, the mind becomes settled and capable; one then cultivates the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) for the sake of accomplishing superior matters, as these are the causes for all desired superior matters.
"Abiding" refers to the mind abiding, which is precisely *samādhi*.

Following the [discussion of] right abandonments, the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) are taught; this refers to the capacity for efficacy, meaning the ability to eliminate five kinds of faults by cultivating the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).
What are the five kinds of faults?
The verse says:
Laziness, forgetting the sacred words, as well as lethargy and restlessness.
Non-application and application—these five faults should be known.
The commentary states:

It should be understood that herein, torpor and restlessness are combined as a single fault; furthermore, it is a fault to fail to apply effort when torpor and restlessness are to be eliminated, or to apply effort again once torpor and restlessness have already been eliminated.
To eliminate these five, one cultivates the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).
How are their characteristics established?
The verse says:
To eliminate indolence, one cultivates desire, diligence, faith, and serenity;
these are the basis and that which relies upon it, as well as the cause and its result.
To eliminate the remaining four faults, one cultivates mindfulness, wisdom, reflection, and equanimity;
noting the words [of the instruction] when recognizing dullness or agitation, one suppresses them through practice until their outflows are extinguished.
The treatise states:
To eliminate laziness, one cultivates the four applications of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*):
first, desire; second, right effort; third, faith; and fourth, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
One should understand that these correspond respectively to the "basis" and so forth.
The "basis" refers to desire (*chanda*), because it is the basis for diligence (*vīrya*).
The "based upon" refers to diligence, because diligence arises in dependence upon desire.
The "causal basis" refers to faith as the proximate cause for the arising of aspiration (*chanda*), because when one has faith and acceptance toward an object, one then develops a longing for it.

The "resultant capacity" refers to serenity (*praśrabdhi*) as the proximate result produced by exertion (*vīrya*), because one who exerts diligent effort attains superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
To counteract the latter four faults, one cultivates the remaining four types of abandonments (prahāṇasaṃskāra) in their respective order:
first, mindfulness; second, clear comprehension; third, volition; and fourth, equanimity.
One should understand that these correspond respectively to "recollection" (*smṛti*) and so forth.
"Recollection" refers to mindfulness, which is able not to forget the object because it records the words of the Noble Ones.

"Awareness of laxity and excitement" refers to correct introspection (*saṃprajanya*), for by means of the recording of recollection, one is able to subsequently recognize the two faults of lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*).

"Subduing practice" refers to volition; having recognized the occurrence of laxity (*laya*) and excitement (*auddhatya*), one initiates an application of effort (*prayoga*) with the desire to subdue and eliminate them.
"Cessation of the outflow" means that once that laxity and excitement have been extinguished, the mind abides in equanimity (*upekṣā*) and flows evenly.
The cultivation of the bases of supernormal power has already been explained; now the cultivation of the five faculties shall be explained.
How are these cultivated five faculties established?
The verse says:
Having already planted the seeds conducive to liberation, one further cultivates the five superior qualities:
namely, aspiration, application, non-forgetfulness, non-distraction, and analytical discernment.
The treatise states:

Through the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the mind becomes capable; once the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) have been fulfilled, one should further cultivate five kinds of supremacy:

first, supremacy of desire; second, supremacy of application; third, supremacy of not forgetting the object; fourth, supremacy of non-distraction; and fifth, supremacy of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*).
These five, in their respective order, are the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) beginning with faith.
Having explained the cultivation of the five faculties, one should now explain the cultivation of the five powers (*pañcabala*). What are the five powers?
What is their sequence?
The verse says:
The very weakening of obstacles is called "power"; Their sequence is established according to cause and effect.
The treatise states:
Those very five faculties previously mentioned—faith and the others—are further designated as "powers" (bala) because they possess superior functional efficacy.
This means they are able to subdue and eliminate hindrances such as lack of faith, and because they cannot be overwhelmed or corrupted by them.
This sequence is established based on cause and effect, because a preceding cause induces a subsequent effect.

That is to say, if one is firmly convinced that cause and effect exist, one will exert diligent effort (*vīrya*) in order to attain that result; having exerted diligent effort, one then abides in right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*); abiding in right mindfulness, the mind attains concentration (*samādhi*); once the mind has attained concentration, one is able to know things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*); and having known them as they truly are, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. Therefore, this sequence is established based on cause and effect.
Once the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) have been perfected as previously described, one further cultivates the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
At what stage does one cultivate the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*):
at the stage of the five faculties or at the stage of the five powers (*pañcabala*)?
The verse says:
Two pairs of factors conducive to penetration reside within the five faculties and the five powers.
The commentary says:

Within the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), the two stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*) occur during the stage of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) occur during the stage of the five powers (*pañcabala*).
Having explained the cultivation of the five powers, one should now explain the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
How are the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) established?
The verse says:
The factors of enlightenment are briefly fivefold: namely, the basis, the intrinsic nature, [the aspect, the function, and the fruit].
Renunciation, benefit, and the three factors free from defilement.
The treatise says:
These factors assist awakening; therefore, they are called factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).
Because these factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are situated on the path of seeing (darśanamārga), they are extensively sevenfold but summarized as five branches.
First is the branch of the basis for awakening, which is mindfulness (smṛti).
Second is the branch of the intrinsic nature of awakening, which is the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya).
The third is the factor of enlightenment of renunciation, which is diligence.
The fourth is the factor of enlightenment of benefit, which is joy.
The fifth is the factor of enlightenment of non-attachment; this further consists of three types, namely tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
For what reason are the three types of non-defilement further explained?
The verse says:
By way of cause, condition, basis, intrinsic nature, and meaning, they are distinguished.
Therefore, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are explained as the factors free from defilement (*asaṃkliṣṭāṅga*).
The treatise says:
Pliancy is itself the causal condition for being free from defilement.
Coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) serves as the cause for the arising of all various defilements, whereas pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is its direct antidote.
The basis refers to concentration (*samādhi*), whose intrinsic nature is equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Therefore, the meaning of being undefiled has three distinct aspects.
Having explained the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) shall now be explained.
How are the factors of the path to be established?
The verse says:
Discrimination and instruction cause others to believe in the three [trainings];
the antidotes to the obstacles are likewise three; therefore, the branches of the path are established as eight.
The treatise says:
The factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are established at the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); therefore, these factors of the path are eight in detail and four in brief.
First, the factor of discernment (*paricchedāṅga*) is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Although this is mundane, it is acquired subsequent to the supramundane [path of seeing], because it is capable of discerning what was personally realized during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Second is the limb of instructing others, which consists of right thought and a portion of right speech, because it involves instructing others by initiating speech.
Third is the limb of causing others to have faith; this has three types, namely right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
The four factors that serve as antidotes to the obstacles also consist of three types, namely right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
By means of these, the path-factors are summarized into four and expanded into eight.
For what reason are the latter two each divided into three?
The verse says:
Manifesting, seeing, and the precepts of detachment, which cause others to have deep faith and acceptance.
Because they serve as antidotes to the root and secondary afflictions, as well as to the obstacles to mastery.
The Commentary says:

Right speech and the other three [right actions] respectively manifest that one has already seen [the truth], possesses the precepts, and is detached, thereby causing others to have faith and acceptance.
That is to say, through right speech and the deliberation of definitive analysis, one causes others to believe and know that one already possesses superior wisdom.

Through right action, one refrains from performing wrong actions, thereby causing others to believe and know that one already possesses pure ethical discipline (*śīla*). Through right livelihood, one seeks robes, alms bowls, and other requisites in accordance with moderation, at the proper time, and in accordance with the Dharma, thereby causing others to believe that one already possesses superior seclusion (*viveka*).
Right effort and the other three [members of the path] respectively counteract the two types of afflictions—the primary and secondary—as well as the obstacle to mastery.
These objects of counteraction are briefly of three kinds:
first, the root afflictions, which are those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Second, the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), namely lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*);
third, the obstacle to mastery (*vaśitā-āvaraṇa*), namely that which obstructs the superior qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are thereby induced.

Among these, right effort (*samyag-vīrya*) specifically serves as the antidote to the first, because it constitutes the diligent cultivation of the path as an antidote to those [secondary afflictions].

Right mindfulness specifically counteracts the second [hindrance], because by fixing the mind and dwelling within the signs of *śamatha* and so forth, one remains far removed from lethargy and restlessness.

Right concentration specifically counteracts the third, because by relying on the sublime meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one is able to swiftly bring forth superior qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
How should the distinctions in cultivation be understood?
The verse says:
With inversion following non-inversion, And non-inversion following inversion.
"Non-erroneous, following the non-erroneous—these are the distinctions in cultivation.
The commentary states:

This cultivation of remedies is briefly of three kinds: first, that which is erroneous but conforms to the non-erroneous; second, that which is non-erroneous but follows the erroneous; and third, that which is non-erroneous and follows the non-erroneous.

These three types of distinctions in cultivation correspond, respectively, to bodhisattvas at the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
How should one understand the distinct characteristics of the remedies cultivated by the two vehicles?
The verse says:
Because the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas are distinguished by their objects of focus,
mental attention, and realizations, they differ from those of the two vehicles.
The treatise states:
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate remedies by taking as their objects the bodies and so forth within their own continuums;
bodhisattvas, however, universally take as their objects the bodies and so forth within both their own and others' continuums while cultivating remedies.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate the antidote by contemplating the body and other objects through the aspects of impermanence and so forth;
whereas bodhisattvas cultivate the antidote by contemplating the body and other objects through the aspect of non-apprehensibility.
When śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cultivate the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, they do so solely for the sake of swiftly attaining dissociation from the body and other aggregates;

whereas when bodhisattvas cultivate the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, it is not for the sake of swiftly attaining dissociation from the body and other aggregates, but rather for the sake of realizing non-abiding nirvāṇa.
The antidotes cultivated by Bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles differ due to these three conditions.
Regarding the general meaning of cultivating antidotes: it refers to cultivation through awakening and cultivation through diminution.
Cultivation of purification;
cultivation of the supreme;
and proximate cultivation, so called because it is proximate to the path of vision (darśanamārga).
Cultivation of realization;
superior cultivation;
cultivation of the initial stage.
Cultivation of the middle stage;
cultivation of the subsequent stage;
cultivation with something superior.
Supreme cultivation refers to the attainment of excellence through the mental engagement with the object of focus.
Chapter Five: Distinguishing the Stages of Cultivation. Having already explained the cultivation of remedies, what are the stages of cultivation?
The verse says:
Regarding the cultivation of remedies that has been explained, there are eighteen stages:
namely, cause, entry, practice, fruit, action, non-action, and excellence;
The superior, the unsurpassed, the stage of practice through understanding, Entering, renunciation, prophecy, teaching,
empowerment, and realization, The benefits, and the performance of activities.
The treatise says:
Regarding the cultivation of various remedies as previously described, there are eighteen distinct stages.
The first is the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*), which refers to the individual (*pudgala*) abiding in the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Second is the stage of entry, which refers to having already generated the resolve for enlightenment.
Third is the stage of application, which refers to having generated the resolve but not yet attained the realization of the fruit.
Fourth is the stage of fruition, which refers to having already attained the fruit.
Fifth is the stage of having something to do, which refers to abiding in the state of one still in training (śaikṣa).
Sixth is the stage of having nothing more to do, which refers to abiding in the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Seventh is the stage of excellence, which refers to having already accomplished various extraordinary qualities such as the supernormal powers (abhijñā).
Eighth is the stage of having a superior position above, which refers to those who have transcended the level of the śrāvakas and others and have already entered the bodhisattva stages.
Ninth is the stage of having no superior position above, which refers to those who have already attained buddhahood, for there is no more exalted stage beyond this.
10. The stage of practice through resolute belief refers to all bodhisattvas on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
11. The stage of entry into realization refers to the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
12. The stage of departure refers to the subsequent six stages.
Thirteenth is the stage of receiving the prediction, which refers to the eighth bhūmi.
Fourteenth is the stage of exposition, which refers to the ninth bhūmi.
Fifteenth is the stage of consecration, which refers to the tenth bhūmi.
Sixteenth is the stage of realization, which refers to the Buddha’s Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Seventeenth is the stage of benefit, which refers to the Enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya).
Eighteenth is the stage of accomplishing what is to be done, which refers to the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).
Although these various distinctions of states are numerous, it should be understood that, in brief, there are only three types.
What are these three?
The verse says:
One should know that within the *dharmadhātu*, there are briefly three stages:
the impure, the pure-and-impure, and the completely pure, as appropriate.
The commentary says:
Regarding the stages of the true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there are briefly three, which subsume all preceding stages as appropriate:
first, the impure stage, which refers to the period from the causal stage up to the stage of application (*prayoga*);
second, the pure-impure stage, which refers to the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).
The three pure stages refer to the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
How should one understand the establishment of individuals (*pudgala*) based on the distinctions among these aforementioned stages?
The verse says:
Based on the various distinctions found within the preceding stages,
one should establish the various *pudgalas* as appropriate.
The treatise says:

One should understand that based on the specific characteristics of the aforementioned stages, the *pudgalas* are established accordingly—namely, that "this one abides in the lineage," "this one has already generated the resolve," and so forth.

Regarding the general meaning of the stages of cultivation: the stage of capability is the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*); the stage of setting forth is the stage of entering the preparatory application (*prayoga*). The stage of impurity, the stage of purity-and-impurity, the stage of complete purity, the stage of being adorned, and the stage of pervasiveness—because it pervades the ten stages—constitute the stage of supremacy (*uttarabhūmi*).
